note: Project recipe knowledge base. The AI's suggest_project / get_recipe tools look things up here. Every project is sized so you can "build something in an afternoon": a visible result first, then the theory. difficulty 1 = only the board is needed; hardware_free = can be run first in the browser's virtual Blue Pill (which only simulates GPIO/PWM/ADC/serial/buttons). Pin conventions: I2C1 PB6/PB7, SPI1 PA5/PA6/PA7, UART1 PA9/PA10, UART2 PA2/PA3, ADC PA0-PA7, onboard LED PC13 lights on LOW, PA0-PA7 are not 5V tolerant. An empty parts.id means the part isn't in the parts library yet and needs to be added with add_part.

projects.title: Let There Be Light: Blinking LED
projects.tagline: Make the little LED on the board go on for a second and off for a second. This is the "Hello World" of all embedded programming. When you're done you'll have a light blinking with a steady rhythm.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

wiring.note: Built into the board, no wiring needed. Lights on LOW

wiring.to: 4 pins at the top of the bluepill
wiring.note: Four wires, one to one. Do not connect 5V

steps: Connect the ST-Link and click Upload in PlatformIO. Result: the terminal shows SUCCESS and the board's LED starts blinking once a second.
Change delay(1000) to delay(100) and flash again. Result: the LED blinks like crazy.
Make the two delays different (on 100, off 900). Result: a "heartbeat" like the one on a router.
Add an external LED on PA1 (with a 220Ω resistor in series). Result: both lights blink together.
Make PA1 and PC13 take turns. Result: the two lights alternate, like police lights.
pitfalls: Upload reports "unknown chip id" / "target voltage may be too low": the ST-Link's 3.3V isn't connected, or you got a clone chip (CH32/GD32). First check whether the board's 3V3 pin has power, then try upload_flags = -c set CPUTAPID 0.
You wrote HIGH but the LED went off: the PC13 LED is wired as a "sink", so LOW turns it on. That's how the board was designed, not your mistake.
Upload succeeded but the LED doesn't blink: check the BOOT0 jumper on the board; it should be on the 0 side.
extensions: Use millis() instead of delay so the board can do other things while blinking
Wire up 3 LEDs and make a chaser
Turn the blink pattern into Morse code and blink out SOS

projects.title: Breathing LED
projects.tagline: The LED is no longer just on or off; it slowly brightens and dims like it's breathing. Once you learn PWM, controlling motor speed and volume work on the same principle.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

steps: Wire up the LED and flash analogWrite(PA1, 128) first. Result: the LED is at half brightness.
Try 255 and 10, flashing once each. Result: full brightness / very dim. Now you see how the number relates to brightness.
Use a for loop 0→255→0. Result: the LED starts breathing.
Change the per-step delay from 10 to 2. Result: the breathing gets faster.
Replace the linear ramp with sin() or a squared curve. Result: the breathing looks more natural (our eyes are more sensitive at the dim end).
pitfalls: analogWrite does nothing, only on/off: the pin you picked doesn't support PWM. On the Blue Pill the PWM-capable pins are PA0-PA3, PA6-PA10, PB0, PB1, PB6-PB9. PC13 can't.
Brightness changes unevenly and the dim part jumps straight to bright: human eyes perceive brightness logarithmically. A curve like b*b/255 looks much smoother.
LED doesn't light: long leg (+) and short leg (-) are swapped. An LED is a diode; it only works one way.
extensions: Make a rainbow fade with an RGB LED
Add a potentiometer so a knob controls the brightness
Rewrite it with millis() so it doesn't block; then you can drop it into any project

projects.title: Button Toggle Light
projects.tagline: Press once for on, press again for off. It looks like the simplest thing, but "button bounce" and "pull-up resistors" are two traps almost everyone falls into once.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

wiring.note: INPUT_PULLUP in code; no external resistor needed

steps: Wire only the button first and print its state to serial. Result: prints 0 when pressed, 1 when released.
LED on while pressed, off when released (follow mode). Result: works like a doorbell button.
Change it to toggle on each press. Result: you'll most likely notice one press sometimes toggles twice. That's bounce.
Add 30ms of debounce. Result: every press toggles exactly once.
Add a 1-second long press that enters breathing mode. Result: short press toggles, long press breathes.
pitfalls: One press makes the light flicker several times, or it works only sometimes: a mechanical button bounces dozens of times the instant it closes. That's called "bounce". Either wait 30ms for it to settle before reading, or use a library.
It lights up randomly without pressing: the pin is "floating" with no pull-up/pull-down, so you're reading random noise. Use INPUT_PULLUP or an external 10k to 3.3V.
Pressing reads 0, not 1: that's how the pull-up wiring works; pressed connects to ground = LOW. Nothing's broken.
extensions: Two buttons: one raises brightness, the other lowers it
Count button presses and print the count to serial
Use attachInterrupt instead of polling

projects.title: Traffic Light
projects.tagline: Red, yellow, and green LEDs cycle with real-intersection timing, plus a "pedestrian button". Your first project with the concept of "state".

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

wiring.note: INPUT_PULLUP in code; no external resistor needed

steps: Wire up the three LEDs and flash a program that lights them in turn. Result: red→yellow→green in sequence, confirming the wiring.
Switch to real timing: green 5 s → yellow 2 s → red 5 s. Result: it feels like a real intersection.
Flash yellow during the last 3 seconds of red (or flash at the end of green). Result: even more like a real intersection.
Add the pedestrian button: pressing it ends the green early. Result: press once and it turns red quickly.
Rewrite it as a state machine (switch/case). Result: the code gets clearer, and adding states doesn't mean starting over.
pitfalls: The three LEDs aren't equally bright: different colors have different forward voltages (red 1.8V, green/blue about 3V), so the same resistor gives different brightness. Swapping the red one to 470Ω evens it out.
The button does nothing in the delay-based version: during delay the CPU does nothing else, so the button never gets read. That's exactly why you learn the millis state machine.
Several LEDs sharing one resistor: they fight over current and the brightness is unstable. One resistor per LED.
extensions: Add a TM1637 7-segment display to show the countdown seconds
Two-direction intersection (6 LEDs) with interlocking
Night mode: flashing yellow

projects.title: Serial Chat
projects.tagline: Type on your computer and the board answers; the board tells the computer how it's doing. Serial is the "eyes and mouth" you'll use for debugging everything from now on.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: USB-to-TTL serial adapter (CH340)
parts.role: Carries what the board says to the computer

steps: Connect the USB-TTL adapter and flash Serial.println("hello"). Result: the serial monitor shows a line of hello every second.
Print millis(). Result: a number that keeps climbing, proving the board is running.
Send characters from the computer and have the board echo them. Result: type a, get a back.
Send "on"/"off" to control the onboard LED. Result: typing switches the light.
Send "temp?" and have the board reply with a fake temperature. Result: you've just built a "command-line protocol".
pitfalls: The serial monitor is blank: on the Blue Pill, Serial defaults to PA9/PA10, not the USB cable. Connect a USB-to-TTL adapter (TX→PA10, RX→PA9, shared GND), or add build_flags = -D USBCON -D USBD_VCP to platformio.ini so Serial goes over USB.
You get garbage like "�����": baud rate mismatch. The code says 115200, so the monitor (monitor_speed in platformio.ini) must be 115200 too.
TX to TX does nothing: serial is "my mouth to your ear". Board TX(PA9) → adapter RX, board RX(PA10) → adapter TX.
Commands do nothing: the monitor isn't set to "append newline on send". The code relies on \n to detect the end of a line.
extensions: Extend the commands to take arguments, like "led 128"
Swap the serial cable for an HC-05 and chat over Bluetooth from your phone
Use Serial2 (PA2/PA3) to make two boards chat with each other

projects.title: Electronic Dice
projects.tagline: Press a button and 7 LEDs "roll" like a real die before landing on 1-6. Learn random numbers and LED patterns.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: 5mm LED
parts.role: Arranged as the 7 pips of a die

wiring.note: By pip position: PA0 top-left, PA1 top-right, PA2 middle-left, PA3 center, PA4 middle-right, PA5 bottom-left, PA6 bottom-right
INPUT_PULLUP in code; no external resistor needed

steps: Arrange 7 LEDs in a die pattern and flash a program that lights them one at a time. Result: you can confirm which LED is in which position.
Write a table: which LEDs light for 1-6. Flash showDice(6). Result: six pips.
Button press → show a random 1-6. Result: different every time (if it's always the same, see pitfall 1).
Add a "rolling" animation: cycle through 15 random faces quickly before settling. Result: it feels like a real roll.
Add a second die (print the second one to serial). Result: you can play Monopoly.
pitfalls: The first roll after power-up is always the same number: random() is pseudo-random, and the same seed gives the same sequence. Seed randomSeed with noise from a floating ADC pin.
The board resets when all 7 LEDs are on: each LED draws about 10mA, and 70mA through the 3V3 regulator is a strain. Use 330Ω resistors or power only from 5V.
The wiring is a rat's nest: sketch the 7 positions and their pins on paper before plugging in wires.
extensions: Draw the pips on an OLED instead
Add a buzzer for clicking sounds while rolling
Two-player mode: whoever rolls higher gets their light flashing

projects.title: Reaction Time Game
projects.tagline: A light comes on at a random moment; press as fast as you can. The board reports your reaction time to the millisecond, and you can compete with friends.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: USB-to-TTL serial adapter (CH340)
parts.role: Carries what the board says to the computer

wiring.note: INPUT_PULLUP in code; no external resistor needed

steps: Wire it up and flash a program that prints millis() when the button is pressed. Result: timestamps show up in the serial monitor.
Wait a random 1-4 seconds, light the LED, then wait for the button. Result: serial prints your reaction time in milliseconds.
Pressing before the light comes on → "false start". Result: no more cheating.
Track and print the best score. Result: you see best after every round.
Add a second button and LED for head-to-head. Result: whoever's faster gets their light.
pitfalls: Reaction time is always 0 or a few milliseconds: the previous press hadn't been released before the next round started. Wait for the button to be released before starting.
Bogus "false start": button bounce got read as a press. Add a 20ms second check.

The serial monitor is blank: on the Blue Pill, Serial defaults to PA9/PA10, not the USB cable. Connect a USB-to-TTL adapter (TX→PA10, RX→PA9, shared GND), or add build_flags = -D USBCON -D USBD_VCP to platformio.ini so Serial goes over USB.
extensions: Show the time on an OLED so you don't need the computer
Use a buzzer instead of a light (audio reaction)
Average 10 rounds and rank the players

projects.title: Night Light (Light Sensor)
projects.tagline: The light comes on automatically when it gets dark, brighter the darker it is, and turns off at dawn. Your first "sensor → decision → action" loop.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: 10kΩ resistor
parts.role: Forms a voltage divider with the photoresistor

wiring.note: The 10k resistor also connects at this point
Photoresistor + 10k form a voltage divider; PA0 reads the midpoint voltage

steps: Wire the divider and print analogRead(PA0) to serial. Result: covering the photoresistor with your hand clearly changes the number (0-1023).
Find the threshold: note the daytime value and the covered value, take the middle. Result: you know your numbers.
LED on when below the threshold. Result: cover it and the light comes on.
Use map() to turn brightness into PWM. Result: the darker it is, the brighter the LED, with a smooth fade.
Add "hysteresis": separate on and off thresholds. Result: the light no longer twitches at the borderline.
pitfalls: The number barely changes: the photoresistor is wired straight to the ADC with no divider resistor. The ADC reads voltage, not resistance; the 10k is what turns resistance changes into voltage changes.
The light flickers wildly at the borderline brightness: it's twitching around a single threshold. Use two thresholds (hysteresis).
As soon as the night light turns on, the sensor thinks it's "bright" and turns it off: it's lighting itself. Point the photoresistor away from the LED, or add hysteresis.
extensions: Swap in a WS2812 strip for a warm ambient light
Add a PIR: only light up when someone is there AND it's dark
Add a potentiometer to tune the threshold on the spot

projects.title: Clap-Activated Light
projects.tagline: Clap once and the light comes on; clap again and it goes off, just like a sound-activated hallway light. When you're done you'll understand why those hallway lights sometimes need a stomp.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: Relay module
parts.role: Optional: control a real desk lamp

wiring.note: Digital output: toggles when there's sound

steps: Wire it up and print the DO pin state to serial. Result: you see 0/1 flip when you clap (if it doesn't, turn the blue potentiometer on the module).
Clap → LED on for 3 seconds, then off. Result: a hallway light.
Change it to toggle on each clap. Result: you'll notice one clap toggles several times.
Add a 500ms lockout. Result: one clap, one toggle.
Add a relay to control a real desk lamp (a low-voltage LED lamp; stay away from wall power). Result: clap to turn on the lamp.
pitfalls: It triggers constantly or never: the potentiometer on the module sets sensitivity. Clap while turning it until the onboard indicator LED "flashes once per clap".
One clap makes the light flicker several times: a single clap is actually a burst of pulses lasting tens of milliseconds. Add a lockout so only one trigger counts per 500ms.
The board freezes/reboots after adding the relay: the relay coil draws a lot of current. Power it from 5V instead of 3V3, and share ground.
extensions: Use the AO analog output to make an LED "volume bar"
Require two claps to trigger (fewer false triggers)
Sound + light control: claps only work when it's dark

projects.title: Ultrasonic Parking Sensor
projects.tagline: The closer you get to an obstacle, the faster the buzzer beeps, just like a car's backup sensor. Learn to measure distance with sound.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

wiring.note: The module needs 5V to be accurate
PB9 is 5V tolerant; Echo is a 5V signal, don't connect it to PA0-PA7

steps: Wire it up and print the distance (cm) to serial. Result: move your hand back and forth and the number follows; check it with a ruler.
Buzzer beeps when the distance is under 50cm. Result: it beeps when something gets close.
Tie the interval to the distance: closer = faster beeps. Result: it feels like a backup sensor.
Continuous tone under 10cm. Result: crash!
Take the median of 5 readings. Result: the number stops jumping around.
pitfalls: Always reads 0 or -1: the module doesn't work on 3.3V; it needs 5V. Or Trig/Echo are swapped.
The value occasionally jumps to 2000+: the ultrasound hit a soft or angled surface and never came back, so it timed out. Take the median of several readings, or ignore values over 400.
Echo connected to PA0-PA7 makes the board hot / kills the pin: those pins are only 3.3V tolerant and Echo is 5V. Use a 5V-tolerant pin like PB8/PB9, or add a 1k series resistor.
The buzzer just clicks instead of beeping: you're using tone() on an active buzzer. An active buzzer sounds when given a HIGH level; only a passive one needs tone().
extensions: Add an OLED to show the distance and a progress bar
Mount it on the front of a robot car for obstacle avoidance
Change it to "the closer, the redder the breathing LED"

projects.title: Door/Motion Alarm
projects.tagline: When someone approaches or the door opens, it instantly sounds an alarm and flashes, with "arm/disarm". Put it by your dorm room door to protect your snacks.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

wiring.note: Output is 3.3V logic; can be connected directly
INPUT_PULLUP; door closed = magnet nearby = switch closed = LOW
INPUT_PULLUP in code; no external resistor needed

steps: Wire the PIR first and print OUT to serial. Result: goes to 1 when someone walks by, back to 0 after a few seconds of stillness.
Someone detected → buzzer for 3 seconds. Result: it sounds as soon as someone walks past.
Add the arm/disarm button, with the LED showing the state. Result: walking past while disarmed does nothing.
Add a 10-second delay after arming (time for you to leave). Result: you can press it and walk out without triggering it yourself.
Add the door sensor: the door opening also triggers the alarm. Result: two sensors, one set of logic.
pitfalls: The PIR triggers several times right after power-up: the module needs 30-60 seconds to warm up and settle, and its output jitters during that time. Wait a minute after power-up before arming.

The PIR says "nobody" when the person stands still: it only senses temperature change (movement), so a still person disappears after a few seconds. That's the principle, not a fault. A jumper on the back of the module selects "repeat trigger" mode.
Too sensitive; a moving curtain sets it off: the PIR has two potentiometers, one for sensitivity (range) and one for delay. Turn the sensitivity down.
Door sensor: the reed switch opens once the magnet is more than 1-2cm away, so mount them on matching spots on the door and frame.
extensions: Put it on the fridge: alarm only if the door sensor is open for more than 60 seconds → fridge-door-left-open reminder
Add an HC-05 to push alerts to your phone over Bluetooth
Add a DS3231 to arm only at night

projects.title: Desk Weather Station (OLED)
projects.tagline: A little screen shows live temperature, humidity, and a small trend line. Nicer on your desk than checking the weather on your phone.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: DHT11 temperature/humidity sensor
parts.role: Sensor (a DHT22 is more accurate and swaps right in)

wiring.note: The module version has a built-in pull-up; a bare sensor needs 10k to 3V3

steps: Wire only the OLED first and run an I2C scan. Result: serial shows 0x3C.
Display "Hello". Result: text on the screen.
Connect the DHT11 and print temperature/humidity to serial. Result: a reading every two seconds; cup the sensor in your hand and the temperature rises.
Draw the data on the OLED in a large font. Result: the beginnings of a desk station.
Store one point per minute and draw a 60-point trend line. Result: you can see the day's temperature trend.
Show "sensor?" when the data is bad (nan). Result: unplugging the wire doesn't crash it.
pitfalls: The OLED stays black: 90% of the time it's the wrong I2C address (0x3C vs. 0x3D) or SDA/SCL swapped. Run the I2C scanner first and don't move on until you see 0x3C.
The DHT keeps reading nan: reading too often (DHT11 needs at least 2 seconds between reads), no pull-up on DATA, or reading right at power-up. delay(2000) before the first read.
Non-ASCII characters show as boxes on the OLED: the Adafruit font is ASCII only. For other character sets, switch to the olikraus/U8g2 library and its fonts (which eat tens of KB of Flash).
Temperature reads 2-3 degrees high: the sensor is right next to the board and getting warmed by the chip and screen. Use jumper wires to move it a bit away.
extensions: Add a BMP280 for barometric pressure and predict rain
Add an ESP-01 to upload readings to your phone
Add a DS3231 to show the time and make it a desk clock

projects.title: Automatic Plant Waterer
projects.tagline: When the soil dries out, the pump runs for a few seconds; when it's wet, it stops. Come back from a week away and your plant is still alive.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: Soil moisture sensor (capacitive)
parts.role: Measures how wet the soil is

parts.name: 1N5819 diode
parts.role: Across the pump to absorb kickback voltage

parts.name: 5V 2A power supply
parts.role: Powers the pump and the board

steps: Connect the soil sensor and print the value to serial. Result: dry soil and wet soil give clearly different numbers; write them down.
Connect the relay and switch it every 3 seconds. Result: you hear clicking and the module's LED blinks.
Hook the pump up to the relay and test it manually first. Result: it pumps water in the right direction.
Write the logic: water for 3 seconds when dry, then wait at least 30 minutes before deciding again. Result: the soil slowly gets wet and the pump stops.
Add "out of water" protection: 5 waterings in a row with no change means alarm and stop. Result: an empty bucket won't burn out the pump.
Switch to the standalone 5V supply and leave it on the windowsill for a day. Result: it's alive.
pitfalls: The relay doesn't click and its LED is half-lit: a 3.3V signal driving a 5V relay module is marginal. Pick an "active-low" module (LOW engages more reliably), or an optocoupler-isolated version.
The board reboots whenever the pump runs: the motor's start/stop current surge drags 5V down. Give the pump its own supply with shared ground only, and put a 1N5819 diode across the pump.
A resistive soil sensor (the two-prong fork) rots in a few days: electrolytic corrosion. Use a capacitive one, or power it only during the second you're measuring.
It waters again right after watering: water takes minutes to reach the sensor. Don't decide right after watering; add a cooldown.
extensions: Add a DS3231 + relay to switch a grow light on a schedule
Add an OLED to show moisture and the time of the last watering
Multiple pots with a multi-channel relay

projects.title: Automatic Pet Feeder
projects.tagline: At 7 AM and 7 PM every day a servo opens the hatch for 1 second to dispense food, and a button gives an extra serving anytime. It doesn't forget the time even after a power outage.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: 1000uF electrolytic capacitor
parts.role: Steadies the voltage when the servo starts

wiring.note: Servo runs on 5V; capacitor goes across 5V/GND
INPUT_PULLUP in code; no external resistor needed

steps: Connect the DS3231 and print the time to serial. Result: you see the date and time ticking (use adjust once the first time).
Connect the servo and write 0°→90°→0°. Result: the servo arm swings back and forth.
Button → servo opens for 1.2 seconds then closes. Result: manual feeding.
Compare the time every minute and feed automatically when it's due. Result: set the time to the next minute to verify.
Remember "already fed this minute" to avoid repeats within the same minute. Result: exactly one feeding at the scheduled time.
Build the hatch mechanism (a bottle + the servo arm). Result: food actually comes out.
pitfalls: The board reboots / serial turns to garbage when the servo moves: the servo draws 500mA+ when it starts and drags the board's 5V down. Power the servo from its own 5V (shared ground) and put a 1000uF capacitor across 5V and GND.

The DS3231 resets to the year 2000 every power-up: no coin cell installed, or a non-rechargeable CR2032 in a module with a charging circuit (it will swell!). DS3231 modules need an LIR2032, or remove the charging resistor.
The servo buzzes and jitters: the target angle hit the end stop (0 or 180). Stay within 10-170.
It fed N times at the scheduled minute: loop runs many times within a minute. Remember "already fed this minute".
extensions: OLED showing the current time and the next feeding time
Add an HX711 load cell to know how much is left in the bowl
Add an HC-05 for remote feeding from your phone

projects.title: Combination Lock (Keypad + Servo)
projects.tagline: Enter a 4-digit code: if it's right, the servo turns the bolt and the green light comes on; three wrong tries locks it for 30 seconds with an alarm.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

wiring.note: 8 header pins; the first 4 are rows

steps: Connect the keypad and print each pressed key to serial. Result: press 5, see 5 (wrong characters mean rows/columns are swapped; fix accordingly).
Beep on every key press. Result: tactile feedback.
Collect 4 digits and compare to the code; green light if correct. Result: serial prints "Unlocked".
Connect the servo: on a correct code, turn 90° for 5 seconds then return. Result: the bolt moves.
3 wrong tries locks it for 30 seconds with flashing red and alarm. Result: brute-force protection.
Press * to clear, # to confirm. Result: feels like a real lock.
pitfalls: Pressing 1 gives 4 or A: rows and columns are swapped or in the wrong order. Test the 8 wires one by one over serial; don't guess.
Some keys don't respond: a matrix keypad relies on scanning, so one loose jumper kills a whole row or column.
The screen/serial goes haywire when the servo turns: power problem, same as the pet feeder.
The code is hard-coded and flashed in; how do you change it? First via a serial command, later by storing it in Flash (EEPROM library).
extensions: Add an OLED to show ****
Add RFID card unlock
Store the code in EEPROM, changeable over serial

projects.title: Pomodoro Timer (OLED + Buttons)
projects.tagline: 25 minutes of work, 5 minutes of rest. Big countdown digits and a progress bar on the screen, and a buzzer when time's up.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

wiring.note: INPUT_PULLUP in code; no external resistor needed

steps: Show "25:00" on the OLED. Result: big digits on the screen.
Count down with millis, refreshing every second. Result: the digits tick.
Button to start/pause. Result: you can stop and resume.
At 0, sound the buzzer and switch to the 5-minute break automatically. Result: a full cycle.
Draw a progress ring/bar. Result: you can see how much is left at a glance.
Second button switches 25/5/custom. Result: it's usable.
pitfalls: The OLED stays black: 90% of the time it's the wrong I2C address (0x3C vs. 0x3D) or SDA/SCL swapped. Run the I2C scanner first and don't move on until you see 0x3C.
The countdown runs slower than your watch: each display() refresh takes tens of milliseconds, and with delay(1000) the error piles up. Use millis differences instead of delay.
You have to press pause several times: the button isn't read during a refresh. Keep refreshes to once a second and read the button on every loop.
The progress bar computes to 0: integer division remain/total rounds to 0 first. Multiply before dividing.
extensions: Add a rotary encoder knob to set the duration
Count today's completed pomodoros and store them in EEPROM
Add a WS2812 ring as the progress ring

projects.title: Digital Thermometer (DS18B20)
projects.tagline: A waterproof probe you can dip in a cup, a fish tank, or your ramen, accurate to 0.1 degrees, shown on serial and an OLED.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

wiring.note: Pull-up resistor; without it you read -127 or 85

steps: Connect the probe + 4.7k and print the temperature to serial. Result: room temperature around 2x.x °C, rising when you hold the probe.
Dip it in ice water. Result: close to 0 degrees, confirming accuracy.
Connect the OLED and show the temperature in big digits. Result: no computer needed.
Track max/min. Result: the screen shows max/min.
Buzzer when it passes 60 °C (the ramen's ready). Result: actually useful.
pitfalls: Reads -127: the probe wasn't found. Almost always the 4.7k pull-up is missing, or the data wire is on the wrong pin.
Reads 85.0: the probe just powered up and hasn't finished its first conversion, or it's underpowered. Wait 1 second before reading, and make sure the red wire is solid.
The three wire colors don't match: some probes are red=VCC, yellow=DATA, black=GND; others mix yellow/white/green. Use a multimeter: the wire that's continuous with the metal shell is GND.
Readings lag after dipping the probe in hot water: the metal shell has thermal inertia. Wait 10 seconds.
extensions: Put 3 probes on the same wire for multi-point measurement
Add a relay to build a temperature-controlled box
Log to an SD card and plot a day's curve

projects.title: Air Quality Monitor (MQ Gas Sensor)
projects.tagline: Detect smoke, alcohol, and flammable gas, with LED colors and a buzzer showing the concentration. The beginnings of a kitchen gas alarm.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: 10kΩ + 20kΩ resistors
parts.role: Voltage divider: brings the 5V output down under 3.3V

wiring.note: Must be 5V; there's a heater inside
Also connect 20kΩ to GND here; AO max 5V→3.3V

steps: Wire it up, power on, and wait 3 minutes to warm up. Result: the module getting warm is normal.
Print the AO value to serial. Result: it settles at a baseline; spray some alcohol or hold a lighter nearby (unlit) and the number jumps.
Set a threshold: baseline × 1.5. Result: green stays on, red when it's over.
Alarm only after 3 seconds continuously over the threshold. Result: a gust of air doesn't cause a false alarm.
Print formatted data to serial and watch the curve in Serial Plotter. Result: you can see the concentration rise and fade.
pitfalls: The value keeps drifting and the threshold is always wrong: MQ sensors have a heater, and a new module needs a 24-48 hour "burn-in" to stabilize, plus a few minutes of warm-up every power-up.
AO straight into PA0 makes the board hot: the MQ-2 runs on 5V and AO goes up to nearly 5V, but ADC pins can only take 3.3V. You must use a divider.
Very low, insensitive readings on 3.3V power: the heater needs 5V or it won't get hot enough to detect anything.
How many ppm is an ADC number? The MQ-2 isn't a precision instrument; calibrate against the curve in the datasheet. For learning, "multiple of the baseline" is good enough.
extensions: Add an OLED with a relative-concentration bar
Add an ESP-01 to push a notification when it's over the limit
Swap in an MQ-135 (CO2/air quality) or MQ-7 (carbon monoxide)

projects.title: Simple Oscilloscope (ADC + Serial Plotter)
projects.tagline: Plot a pin's voltage as a live waveform. Turn a potentiometer and watch the line go up and down; probe a breathing LED and see the PWM sawtooth.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: USB-to-TTL serial adapter (CH340)
parts.role: Carries what the board says to the computer

parts.name: 10kΩ potentiometer
parts.role: Produces a variable voltage as the signal source

parts.name: Capacitor (any value)
parts.role: For viewing the RC charge/discharge curve

wiring.to: Probe output: analogWrite generates PWM for you to measure
wiring.note: Optional; try connecting it to PA0 through a 1k resistor

steps: Connect the potentiometer and print analogRead(PA0) to serial every 10ms. Result: Serial Plotter (or a VS Code serial-plot extension) shows a line that moves as you turn the knob.
Print the voltage instead (v * 3.3 / 1023). Result: the axis becomes real volts.
Have PA1 output PWM and connect it to PA0 through a 1k resistor. Result: you see a square wave/sawtooth (it looks like a sawtooth if the sample rate is too low).
Add an RC (10k + capacitor) in front of PA0. Result: the square wave turns into a rounded charge/discharge curve. That's a low-pass filter.
Set analogReadResolution to 12 bits. Result: a finer curve (0-4095).
pitfalls: The curve looks like a "sawtooth"/a blob: the sample rate is too low to show the real PWM (PWM is about 1kHz; sampling at 500Hz only shows aliasing). An oscilloscope is all about sample rate.
Printing too fast freezes the display: at 115200 baud, serial can move about 1000 lines per second at most. Don't print every microsecond.
Measuring a 5V signal killed the board: ADC pins max out at 3.3V. Divide higher voltages first (10k + 20k handles up to 5V).
Readings drift: the ADC reference is the 3.3V regulator output, so an unstable USB supply makes it drift.
extensions: Draw the waveform directly on an OLED for a portable scope
Add a trigger (start recording only above a certain voltage)
Record to an SD card and analyze on the computer

projects.title: Smart Fan (Temperature-Controlled PWM)
projects.tagline: The hotter it gets, the faster the fan spins; it stops when things cool down, and you can adjust it by hand. The same logic as laptop cooling.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: DC motor (just the small motor + fan blade from the kit)

wiring.note: PWM; PA8 is a TIM1 channel

steps: Connect the MOSFET module and motor, then analogWrite(PA8, 255). Result: the motor runs at full speed.
Add analogWriteFrequency(25000) and then write 128. Result: half speed, and no whining noise.
Connect the DS18B20 and print the temperature. Result: normal readings.
Map temperature → speed (stop at 25 °C, full speed at 35 °C). Result: hold the probe and the fan speeds up.
Let the potentiometer take over as manual mode (all the way down = auto). Result: two modes.
Minimum starting duty cycle: below 30% the motor won't turn. Result: no more "powered but stalled".
pitfalls: The motor just hums or runs very slowly: the IRF520 isn't a "logic-level" MOSFET, so 3.3V only half-opens it. Use a logic-level MOSFET module like IRLZ44N/AO3400, or an L298N.
A sharp whine at half speed: the default PWM (about 1kHz) is within hearing range. Use analogWriteFrequency(25000).
The board reboots the instant the motor stops: a motor is an inductor and kicks back when power is cut. Put a diode across it and a capacitor on the supply.
The temperature reading keeps climbing: the probe is next to the motor/MOSFET and getting heated.
extensions: Add an OLED to show temperature and speed
Switch to a 4-wire PC fan and read its RPM (FG wire)
Turn it into an add-on fan controller for a PC case

projects.title: Bluetooth RC Car
projects.tagline: Install a Bluetooth serial app on your phone, tap forward/back/left/right, and the car moves. Your first project that actually drives.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: 2x DC motors + L298N driver + car chassis

wiring.note: Leave the onboard regulator jumper in place; its 5V output can power the Blue Pill
PWM left wheel speed (remove the jumper cap)
The module has its own regulator; 3.3V logic

steps: Before mounting the wheels, connect the motors to the L298N and write forward 2 seconds, backward 2 seconds. Result: both motors spin the same way (if one is reversed, swap its IN pins).
Connect the HC-05, pair from the phone app (PIN 1234), send characters, and echo them on serial. Result: phone sends F, board receives F.
Map F/B/L/R/S to forward/back/left/right/stop. Result: the phone controls the wheels.
Digits 0-9 set the speed. Result: slow and fast.
Stop if no command arrives for 500ms. Result: the car doesn't run away if Bluetooth drops.
Mount the wheels and drive. Result: zooming around the room.
pitfalls: The phone can't find the HC-05: the module LED must blink fast to be pairable; slow blinking means already connected. The HC-05 is Classic Bluetooth, which iPhones don't support; use Android.
Everything from the HC-05 is garbage: the baud rate isn't 9600 (someone entered AT mode and changed it to 38400), or TX/RX are swapped.

The Blue Pill reboots as soon as the motors run: too much motor noise. Charge the batteries, feed the board from the L298N's 5V output, add a big capacitor, and don't run two motors from a single 18650.
The L298N gets hot and the motors are weak: it drops over 2V internally, so 7.4V in leaves the motors only about 5V. That's normal; for more power switch to a TB6612.
extensions: Add an ultrasonic sensor in front for obstacle avoidance
Use a phone-app joystick for proportional control
Add WS2812 headlights

projects.title: Line-Following Car
projects.tagline: Lay out a track with black tape on white paper, and the car follows the line by itself, no remote needed.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: TCRT5000 infrared line sensor module
parts.role: Sees the black line on the floor (one left, one right)

steps: Connect the two line sensors and print both DO pins to serial. Result: 1 over black tape, 0 over white paper (if reversed, just treat it as reversed).
Adjust the module potentiometers so the sensors clearly distinguish black/white at 1cm off the floor. Result: stable readings.
Simple logic: both white = straight, left black = turn left, right black = turn right. Result: follows straight lines and gentle curves.
Both black = finish line, stop. Result: it stops at the end.
Slow the inner wheel instead of stopping it in turns. Result: smoother driving.
Line lost (both white for over 1 second) → search in the last direction. Result: it doesn't wander off.
pitfalls: The sensor reads the same over black and white: it's too high off the floor (>2cm) or the potentiometer isn't adjusted. Ideal height is 0.5-1.5cm; turn the pot while watching the module's indicator LED.
The car keeps zigzagging: too fast, or the sensors are spaced much narrower than the line. Slow down and space the sensors slightly wider than the tape.
It fails in bright light: infrared in sunlight "blinds" the sensors. Use it indoors or add a shade.
It veers as soon as you add batteries: the two motors were never equally fast. Calibrate left and right PWM separately.
extensions: Use a 5-channel line sensor + PID control for fast, stable following
Add an ultrasonic sensor to stop for obstacles
Count intersections and turn at the Nth one

projects.title: Infrared Remote Switch
projects.tagline: Use your TV remote (or the one from the kit) to switch a desk lamp or fan, with each button doing one thing.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

steps: Connect the receiver, flash the library's receive example, and press remote buttons. Result: serial prints each button's code (write them down).
Put the codes in your code; button 1 turns on LED1. Result: remote-controlled light.
Button 2 turns on LED2, button 0 turns everything off. Result: multiple button mappings.
Holding a button triggers repeatedly → handle the "repeat code". Result: one press toggles exactly once.
Add a relay to control a 5V desk lamp. Result: remote-controlled lamp.
pitfalls: Nothing is received: the receiver's three pins are in different orders from different makers (commonly OUT-GND-VCC), and wiring it backwards makes it heat up. Check the module's markings or datasheet.
The same button gives a different code every time / you see 0xFFFFFFFF: that's the "repeat code", meaning the button is being held. Check the flags and ignore it.
False triggers under fluorescent lights/sunlight: the 38kHz carrier gets interfered with. Keep away from strong light sources.
Compile error: IRremote.h not found: version 4.x renamed the header to IRremote.hpp; older tutorials use .h.
extensions: Add an IR emitter LED to build a universal remote for a real TV
Combine with a photoresistor: use the remote to set an auto mode
Show which channels are on with an OLED

projects.title: Pedometer (MPU6050)
projects.tagline: Strap it to your leg or hold it while walking, and the OLED shows your step count. Learn to read acceleration and pick out a "step" from the "shaking".

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

wiring.note: Both modules on the same I2C bus (addresses 0x68 / 0x3C don't clash)
INPUT_PULLUP in code; no external resistor needed

steps: I2C scan. Result: you see both addresses, 0x68 and 0x3C.
Print ax ay az to serial. Result: lying flat az≈9.8; flip it and it goes negative.
Compute the acceleration magnitude |a| and watch the walking waveform in Serial Plotter. Result: a clear peak for every step.
Peak detection: above the threshold and >300ms since the last one = one step. Result: walk 20 steps, count 18-22.
Big step count on the OLED, button resets to zero. Result: usable.
Power it from the battery, put it in your pocket, and take a walk. Result: real step counting.
pitfalls: MPU6050 not found: the module's AD0 pin is tied high, changing the address to 0x69; or the 3.3V supply is weak. Confirm the address with an I2C scan.
It counts steps while sitting still: the threshold is too low, or you're looking at one axis instead of the magnitude. The threshold should be 2-3 above the resting 9.8.
One arm swing counts as several steps: add a minimum interval (300ms); people take at most 3 steps per second.
The OLED glitches with two devices on I2C: jumper wires too long, pull-ups too weak. Shorten the wires, or Wire.setClock(100000).
extensions: Add calorie/distance estimates
Store daily steps in EEPROM and reset at midnight with a DS3231
Use the gyroscope for "flip your wrist to wake the screen"

projects.title: Water Level / Leak Alarm
projects.tagline: Put it next to the washing machine or by the fish tank; as soon as water reaches the sensor it sounds off. It can also show the water level in a cup or tank.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

wiring.note: Powered from a GPIO so it's only on while measuring, to prevent corrosion
ADC; output stays under 3.3V when powered from 3.3V

steps: Wire it up and print AO to serial. Result: near 0 when dry (or 1023, depending on the module), changing when wet.
Stand the sensor in a cup and slowly add water. Result: the value changes roughly linearly with the level; note three thresholds.
Three LEDs show low/mid/high. Result: the lights come on one by one as you add water.
High level (or any water) triggers the buzzer. Result: leak alarm.
Switch to intermittent GPIO power (on for 50ms every 2 seconds to measure). Result: the electrodes no longer turn black within days.
pitfalls: Readings drop over a few days and the electrodes turn black: constant power while submerged causes electrolytic corrosion. Power it from a GPIO and only for the 30ms you're measuring.
Dry readings aren't 0 but jump around: floating electrodes pick up noise. Treat anything below 50 as 0 in code.
AO exceeds 3.3V on 5V power: ADC pins max out at 3.3V. Powering the sensor from 3V3 or a GPIO keeps it safe.
Tap water and purified water read very differently: the sensor measures conductivity, not true "level". Calibrate with the same water you'll use.
extensions: Add an HC-05 to push leak alerts to your phone
Add a relay to shut off a pump / start a drain pump automatically
Switch to a non-contact XKC-Y25 level sensor stuck to the outside of the tank

projects.title: Automatic Curtain (Servo Window)
projects.tagline: Opens automatically at dawn, closes at dusk, and a button toggles it by hand. Build a small model window first, then upgrade to real curtains.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: MG996R metal-gear servo
parts.role: Upgrade: for pulling real curtains (much stronger)

wiring.note: INPUT_PULLUP in code; no external resistor needed

steps: Servo 0°↔180° back and forth. Result: the arm swings; figure out which angle is "open" and which is "closed".
Button toggles open/closed. Result: a manual curtain.
Print the photoresistor value and find the day/night threshold. Result: you know your numbers.
Bright→open, dark→close, with hysteresis and a 1-minute confirmation (a passing cloud isn't nightfall). Result: no twitching.
Move the servo slowly (1° every 15ms). Result: it draws the curtain like a person would, not with a "snap".
No automatic moves for 30 minutes after a manual one. Result: the human has the final say.
pitfalls: The curtain opens when you turn on the room light at night: the photoresistor is seeing indoor light. Stick it facing the window, or add the "60-second persistence" check.
The servo can't reach its position and buzzes: it's stuck or past its travel. Don't write 0/180 to an SG90; use 10-170.
An SG90 can't pull a real curtain: it only has 1.8kg·cm of torque. For real curtains use an MG996R or a stepper motor with its own 5V 2A supply.
The servo keeps twitching after it arrives: supply noise. Put 1000uF across 5V/GND, or detach() once it's in position.
extensions: Switch to a 28BYJ-48 stepper to drive a real curtain track
Add a DS3231 schedule: open at 7 AM on weekdays
Add an HC-05 for phone control

projects.title: Mini Piano (Passive Buzzer)
projects.tagline: 8 buttons become 8 piano keys that play do re mi when pressed; when nobody's playing, it plays "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" on its own.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

wiring.to: One leg of each of the 8 buttons
wiring.note: INPUT_PULLUP; they map to C D E F G A B C5

steps: First flash tone(PA1, 440) for 1 second. Result: you hear a standard A note.
Wire one button; pressing it plays 262Hz (C). Result: one piano key.
8 keys, 8 frequencies. Result: you can play a scale.
Write a melody array (notes + durations) that plays on power-up. Result: "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star".
Add volume (really just duty cycle): try analogWrite instead of tone. Result: you'll find the passive buzzer's volume really does change a little.
pitfalls: It only "beeps" at one pitch: you bought an active buzzer. An active one has its own oscillator and makes one tone; only a passive one can change pitch with tone(). To tell them apart: an active buzzer's back is sealed with black epoxy; on a passive one you can see the green circuit board.
It's very quiet: a passive buzzer driven straight from a GPIO gets only a few milliamps. Add an NPN transistor (S8050) driver and it gets much louder.
Pressing two keys plays only one: one buzzer can only make one frequency at a time. That's a physical limit, hence the break in the code.
The melody runs together: no gaps between notes. Call noTone for a few tens of milliseconds after each note.
extensions: Add a potentiometer to shift octaves
Add an OLED to show the current note name
Convert MIDI or sheet music into an array and play any song

projects.title: Digital Clock (DS3231 + 7-Segment Display)
projects.tagline: A 4-digit red 7-segment display shows hours:minutes with a colon that blinks every second. It keeps time through power loss and has an alarm.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

wiring.note: INPUT_PULLUP in code; no external resistor needed

steps: Show 1234 on the display. Result: it lights up, confirming CLK/DIO aren't swapped.
Print the DS3231 time to serial and calibrate it once from the compile time. Result: the time is ticking.
Show HH:MM on the display with the colon blinking every second. Result: a clock.
Long-press button 1 to enter time-setting; button 2 adds a minute. Result: you can set it.
Set an alarm time; when it's due the buzzer sounds until any key is pressed. Result: it can wake you up.
Dim the display automatically at night. Result: easy on the eyes.
pitfalls: The display is dark or garbled: the TM1637 is not an I2C device, so don't put it on PB6/PB7 fighting with the DS3231; swapped CLK/DIO is another common cause.

The time runs slow/fast compared to your phone: the DS3231 itself is very accurate (under 1 minute a year); what's off is the compile-time setting, which includes the ten-odd seconds between compiling and finishing the upload. Once set, don't adjust again.
The time resets every time you re-flash: the code calls rtc.adjust() unconditionally. Only set it when lostPower() is true.
Time is lost even after replacing the coin cell: the module's charging circuit + a non-rechargeable CR2032 "charged" the battery to death.
extensions: Add a DHT11 and alternate between time and temperature
Add a photoresistor for automatic brightness
Switch to an OLED to show the date and weekday

projects.title: RFID Door Access
projects.tagline: Tap a card to open the door: cards on the allow list unlock the servo with a green light; unknown cards get a red light and alarm, and every tap is logged to serial.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

parts.name: RC522 RFID module + blank card + key fob

steps: Connect the RC522 and run the read-UID example. Result: tapping a card prints a 4-byte UID to serial (like A3 5F 12 9C).
Put your own card's UID in the allow list. Result: tapping your card prints "Welcome".
Connect the servo: a valid card turns it 90° for 3 seconds, then back. Result: an unlock action.
Green light + two short beeps / red light + one long low tone. Result: you know the result without looking at serial.
3 unknown cards in a row trigger a 10-second alarm. Result: tamper protection.
Print timestamped log lines to serial (add a DS3231). Result: an access log.
pitfalls: RC522 fried on 5V: the module is 3.3V only; the pin labeled 3.3V is its maximum. Its logic level is 3.3V too, a perfect match for the Blue Pill.
No cards read, firmware version prints 0x00 or 0xFF: SPI wiring is wrong or the jumper wires are too long. MOSI/MISO can't be swapped, and keep wires under 15cm.
One card tap triggers several times: PICC_HaltA() wasn't called, so the card stays in the field.
Your phone's NFC isn't detected: the RC522 only supports 13.56MHz MIFARE cards; 125kHz ID cards used by some access systems can't be read (you'd need an RDM6300).
extensions: Add an "admin card": after tapping it, the next card gets added to the allow list and saved to EEPROM
Add an OLED to show the name and time
Connect an electromagnetic lock (12V + relay) for a real door

projects.title: GPS Logger (Advanced)
projects.tagline: Take it biking or hiking: the OLED shows live latitude/longitude and speed, the track is written to an SD card every second, and at home you import it into a map app to see your route.

parts.name: ST-Link V2 programmer
parts.role: Flashes the program onto the board

wiring.note: The GPS only talks, never listens; one wire is enough
Chip select, your choice of pin
The module has a regulator; a bare SD socket takes 3V3
INPUT_PULLUP in code; no external resistor needed
An 18650's 3.7V straight into the 3V3 pin is wrong either way; use a module with a 5V boost converter

steps: Connect the GPS to USART2 and forward the raw NMEA to Serial as-is. Result: a stream of $GPRMC,$GPGGA text. Go to a window or outside and wait 1-5 minutes for coordinates to appear.
Parse it with TinyGPS++ and print latitude/longitude, satellite count, and speed to serial. Result: human-readable data.
Test the SD module alone: write a line of hello and read it back. Result: the file shows up when you read the card on your computer.
Show latitude/longitude/speed/satellites on the OLED. Result: no computer needed.
Button starts recording; write one CSV line per second (time,lat,lng,speed). Result: a file is created as you walk around.
Convert the CSV to GPX on your computer and import it into a map app. Result: you see your own track.
pitfalls: Stuck on searching: a cold-start GPS almost never gets a fix indoors. Go to a window or outside; the first fix can take 5-15 minutes. When the module's LED starts blinking, it has a fix.
NMEA arrives but latitude/longitude are all 0: no fix yet (the status in $GPRMC is V). Wait for 4 or more satellites.

SD init fails / the file has only the header and no data: init failures are usually a card that isn't FAT32, jumper wires too long (drop SPI to 4MHz), or unstable module power. Header but no data means power was cut before sync()/close(), so the data was still in the buffer. sync after every write.
Out of Flash (region FLASH overflowed): the three libraries together exceed 64KB. Most C8T6 chips actually have 128KB; add board_upload.maximum_size = 131072 to platformio.ini, or drop the OLED.
concepts: SPI and the SD card file system
I2C + SPI + UART on one board
extensions: Add an MPU6050 to record how bumpy the ride is
Add an ESP-01 to upload your position live
Compute total distance and average speed and show them on the screen
